items.title: Biodiversity Risk in the Corporate Bond Market
items.abstract: We show that a biodiversity risk premium has emerged in the U.S. corporate bond market following the United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP15) in October 2021. COP15 placed biodiversity on the global regulatory agenda and raised transition risks for exposed firms. After COP15, a one standard deviation increase in a firm’s biodiversity footprint is associated with a 7% increase in its secondary market yield spreads, whereas this relation is insignificant before COP15. The biodiversity effect is also present in primary bond markets, most pronounced for medium-term bonds and distinct from climate-related mechanisms. Furthermore, a higher biodiversity footprint is associated with a lower likelihood of issuing medium-term bonds after COP15, consistent with firms managing their biodiversity-related risks. Evidence from firms’ biodiversity dependencies suggests that physical biodiversity risks are also priced in the bond market. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07660 .

items.title: Whiplash: Congestion Dissipation in a Disrupted Circulatory Shipping System
items.abstract: The (post)pandemic period was marked by numerous port disruptions, leading to delays and rising costs for shippers. We build a fluid model in transient states to investigate how a disruption at one port can affect the disrupted port and its counterpart in another country in a circulatory container shipping system, where a stream of fleets moves goods back and forth between the two ports. Port disruption leads to two types of congestion: the inbound backlogs, which occur when ships are unable to enter the port, and the outbound backlogs, which arise when goods are unable to be loaded onto ships for transport to other ports. We analytically characterize the system’s recovery time, measured from the onset of the port closure until normal operations are restored, and the dynamics of inbound and outbound backlogs during recovery. We identify a whiplash effect in which outbound backlogs alternate between ports, creating oscillatory congestion patterns because of the disruption-induced uneven spatial distribution of ships. Our analysis reveals that simply increasing ship capacity may not expedite system recovery, highlighting the importance of coordination between port authorities and shipping companies when jointly planning capacity expansions. Furthermore, we examine several extensions of the model. We use the two-port system as a building block to analyze bipartite and cyclic network structures, and we also consider scenarios in which a port experiences multiple disruptions. In all cases, the whiplash effect persists, thereby demonstrating the robustness of our findings. Finally, we use our theory model prediction as a feature and apply machine learning techniques to predict the time that vessels spend in Shanghai Port after a typhoon disruption and show that using our model predictor, alongside all relevant vessel and voyage attributes as raw features, significantly reduces prediction errors by 10%–30% on average compared with not using it. This paper was accepted by Elena Katok, operations management. Funding: This work was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada [Grant RGPIN-2021-04295]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05427 .

items.title: Do Fund Managers’ Commitments to Responsible Investing Affect Private Information Acquisition, Information Environment, and Corporate Sustainability?
items.abstract: We investigate the effects of mutual funds’ commitments to responsible investing on their information acquisition activities and the corresponding externalities for other stakeholders. After committing to responsible investing (via United Nations Principles for Responsible Investment (UNPRI)), fund managers increase private information acquisition activities, that is, corporate site visits, particularly focusing on environmental and social issues. These visits generate negligible private investment value for the visiting funds. However, the information environment at the stock level improves following these visits with lower consensus analyst forecast errors. In addition to the information production role of these visits, they also generate positive externalities for other stakeholders through incremental improvements in the sustainability practices of the firms receiving sustainability-focused site visits from UNPRI fund managers. Collectively, the paper highlights the private costs and social benefits of responsible investing. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal and J. Sulaeman acknowledge research support from Sustainable and Green Finance Institute [Grant WBS A-0006413-00-00]. Y. Zhang acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72402239] and China Scholarship Council. This work was supported by the Ministry of Education, Singapore [Social Science and Humanities Research Thematic Grant SSRC2024-SSHRTG-022]. items.title: Advertising by Recruiting Influencers
items.abstract: The rise of social media platforms has enabled customers to rely on influencers and peer reviews to guide their purchasing decisions. As products increasingly focus on experiences, firms are leveraging influencer marketing as a crucial tool. This paper addresses key challenges of influencer marketing by considering different types of influencers and partnership schemes alongside the impact of social learning. We introduce a two-period model wherein, in the initial period, the firm unveils a new product experience of unknown quality alongside an influencer marketing campaign. The campaign relies on two types of influencers that differ in popularity and engagement levels and two partnerships: sponsored advertising and public relations. Customers base their purchasing decisions on their original (heterogeneous) beliefs, influencer-driven information, and reviews from early adopters in the second period. When customers are equally likely to follow any given influencer, the firm should choose a single influencer type and partnership. Consumer reviews complement influencer marketing when products are initially undervalued, increasing the returns to influencer investment. Moreover, within a societal structure characterized by distinct classes, in which followers and influencers often belong to the same class, a mix of influencer types and partnership schemes may become optimal. Our study provides guidance on selecting influencer types, partnership schemes, and social media platforms based on engagement, popularity, audience composition, and platform characteristics. This paper was accepted by Jeanette Song, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07919 .

items.title: A Credit Risk Assessment Model Based on SVM With a Hypersphere‐Based Adaptive Oversampling Technique
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Credit risk prediction for small and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs) is challenging under imbalanced data conditions, where the scarcity of high‐risk SME samples undermines the performance of traditional classifiers. However, SME credit risk studies addressing data imbalance have mainly focused on class imbalance, while other performance‐degrading data difficulty factors, such as outliers, small disjuncts, and class overlap, remain underexplored. To address these challenges, we develop a customized credit risk assessment framework, termed DCHO‐SVM, that integrates the DCHO oversampling method for data preprocessing with SVM for classification. The model first employs principal component analysis (PCA) to reduce data dimensionality and derives a compact feature representation from the constructed indicator system. Subsequently, DCHO preprocesses the training data by dynamically constructing hyperspheres, adaptively determining their oversampling weights based on local distribution characteristics to address within‐class imbalance, and then performing oversampling within the hyperspheres to avoid class overlap. Finally, the balanced training set obtained after oversampling is used to train the SVM classifier, which is subsequently utilized for SME credit risk prediction. Empirical analysis on 551 Chinese listed manufacturing SMEs shows that the proposed model outperforms the conventional classifier, with , , , , and improving from 0.741, 0.507, 0.763, 0.602, and 0.455 to 0.924, 0.752, 0.935, 0.920, and 0.734, respectively. In addition, robustness tests on various real‐world imbalanced credit datasets from UCI and Fannie Mae repositories further verify the effectiveness and generalizability of the proposed model. These results indicate that DCHO‐SVM provides an effective solution for SME credit risk assessment under complex imbalanced scenarios.
